## Where we are

Over the next two lectures we build models. Before that, a step back: what actually happens around a model when you do a data science project?

::: {.callout-important title="Recall from everything we know"}
Last week we learned about how to come up with a good research question and how to import data. And previously we have done a lot of work on data tidying, transformation, and visualization. So what is next?
:::


:::{.callout-note title="Today's Agenda"}

- the workflow behind a data science project
- a live project from scratch
:::

## Give me something!

::: {.callout-important title="Scenario"}
Imagine your manager comes to you and hands youa usb stick containing a data set. They say: *"Find something useful in here."* What are you supposed to do?
:::

![](https://en.meming.world/images/en/c/c7/Confused_Nick_Young.jpg){fig-align="center" width="40%"}


## The data project workflow

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-width: 8
flowchart LR
  A[Question] --> B[Data]
  B --> C[Clean]
  C --> D[Explore]
  D --> E[Model]
  E --> F[Communicate]
  D -.->|new question| A
  E -.->|new question| A
```

::: {.callout-tip}
Each arrow can point backwards too. Exploring the data often changes the question.
:::

## Most of the work is not the model

::: {.callout-note title="A common surprise"}
In practice, most of the time goes into the steps **around** the model: understanding the question, getting the data, cleaning it, and looking at it.
:::

- A model built on a vague question answers the wrong thing, very precisely.
- A model built on data you do not understand is hard to trust.
- Communication is part of the job: a result nobody understands changes nothing.


## Start with the question {.smaller}

The same data set can answer very different questions. The kind of question decides what you do next.

| Type | What it asks | Example |
|---|-------|-------|
| Descriptive | What does the data look like? | What is the average sleep per night? |
| Exploratory | What patterns are in here? | Do some programs sleep more than others? |
| Inferential | Is a pattern real, and how big is it? | Is sleep related to grades? |
| Predictive | What will a new value be? | What grade would we expect for someone sleeping 7 hours? |

::: {.callout-note title="Looking ahead"}
Lecture 16 and 17 are about models. A model can serve the inferential and predictive questions, and it can also describe a pattern. At this stage I don't expect you to ask these types of questions yet, but it doesn't hurt to think ahead!
:::


## Know your data

::: {.callout-caution title="Questions to ask about any dataset"}
1. Who collected it, and why?
2. Who is in it? Who is missing?
3. How was each variable measured? Self-reported, or recorded by a device?
4. When was it collected? Is it still relevant?
5. Does it contain anything unrealistic (impossible values, strange units, missing values coded as 0)?
:::

A clean-looking spreadsheet can still hide a biased sample or a measurement problem.



# Let's practice! 



## Reflection

::: {.callout-caution title="Think about what you just saw"}
1. What was the question at the start? Did it change?
2. What did we do at each stage of the workflow?
3. What surprised us, and how did we respond?
4. What would make you doubt our conclusion?
:::

## Good practice 

::: {.callout-important title="Make your work reproducible"}
Keep your steps in a script or document, not in your head. Someone else (including you, next month) should be able to rerun everything.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Document your decisions"}
Write down why you removed or changed anything. Never drop values just because they are inconvenient, and disclose what you removed.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Report honestly"}
Say what the data can and cannot tell you.
:::
